title: Santa Fe Institute Research Bridge

hero.headline: When does local structure survive promotion to the next scale?
hero.support: Boundary First Labs is studying emergence as invariant-preserving promotion across changing representations and scales. The useful question for complex-systems research is not whether the vocabulary sounds compatible, but whether it yields measurable structure that survives comparison with established multiscale methods.

researchBridge: Distinction spaces ask how meaningful states become available and how those distinctions are sourced.
Emergence work asks when local or mesoscopic closure residues can be promoted into higher-level primitives without losing the invariant that made them meaningful.
Representational Mechanics asks what structure survives when the same system is modeled at different scales, resolutions, or carriers.
Admissibility provides a candidate discipline for distinguishing lawful coarse-graining or abstraction from information loss that invalidates downstream inference.
candidateStudies: Compare a Boundary First promotion model with an established multiscale or coarse-graining analysis on one bounded complex system.
Test whether defect concentration or boundary structure identifies transitions that are already captured by standard observables, and preserve a null result if it does not.
Study when two representations of the same system are formally adequate but operationally asymmetric in the transitions they expose.
Build a small cross-scale casebook in which local closure, mesoscopic residue, promotion, and macro-interface formation can be independently annotated and criticized.
firstAsk: Choose one multiscale system where the relevant coarse-graining is already well understood and test whether the Boundary First promotion language adds anything measurable, compressive, or explanatory.
claimBoundary: This page does not imply Santa Fe Institute endorsement, partnership, affiliation, or review.
Compatibility with complex-systems language is not evidence of a new result.
Boundary First must benchmark against established multiscale, network, dynamical-systems, information-theoretic, and statistical approaches appropriate to the selected system.
A clean reduction or null result is a valid outcome and should narrow the theory.
